people.label: Leonard H. Stringfield
people.sub: Founder, CRIFO; MUFON director of public relations; author, UFO Crash/Retrieval Status Reports I-VII
people.narrative: Leonard H. Stringfield (1920-1994) is the origin point of the crash-retrieval literature as a body of work rather than a rumour. A former Army Air Forces intelligence officer in the Pacific in World War II, he founded CRIFO (Civilian Research, Interplanetary Flying Objects) in Cincinnati in the 1950s and served 1967-1969 as an Early Warning Coordinator feeding sighting reports to the Condon Committee, which put him inside the official investigative loop before he turned on it. After references to crashes and recovered bodies in his 1977 Doubleday book 'Situation Red, The UFO Siege' produced an unexpected flow of new informants, he delivered 'Retrievals of the Third Kind: A Case Study of Alleged UFOs and Occupants in Military Custody' at the ninth annual MUFON Symposium in Dayton, Ohio, on 29 July 1978. That paper opened the modern retrieval literature and he then produced six further Status Reports between January 1980 and February 1994, each a numbered, dated, case-coded compilation of testimony from sources he anonymised behind letter-number codes. His method is the load-bearing weakness and the load-bearing strength of the whole field: he protected sources absolutely, which is why they talked to him, and which is also why almost nothing he published can be independently audited. Stringfield himself said so, opening Status Report IV with a section titled 'The Burden of Proof' in which he wrote that 'we, in the domain of public research, do not have that exalted proof' and that affidavits, leaked documents and photographs do not constitute proof. He worked with the Fund for UFO Research, MUFON, CUFOS and the Mid-Ohio Research Associates, and Richard Hall edited Status Report VI. He died of lung cancer on 18 December 1994, ten months after the last report.

people.tierRationale: He created the source corpus that every later crash-retrieval researcher cites. Tier A for centrality to the record even though almost all of his own sourcing is anonymous and therefore tier 2 or 3 by this board's grading.

people.label: Stanton T. Friedman
people.sub: Nuclear physicist; first civilian Roswell investigator; MJ-12 researcher
people.narrative: Stanton Terry Friedman (29 July 1934 - 13 May 2019) was a nuclear physicist who spent fourteen years on classified nuclear propulsion programmes at General Electric, Aerojet General Nucleonics, General Motors, Westinghouse, TRW and McDonnell Douglas before leaving full-time physics in 1970 to investigate UFOs professionally. That industrial background matters to this board: Friedman had held clearances on compartmented nuclear aircraft and fission and fusion rocket work, and he argued from direct experience that a programme could be run for decades without leaking, because he had worked inside ones that did not. In February 1978 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, he was put in touch with Major Jesse A. Marcel Sr., the 509th Bomb Group intelligence officer who had handled the Roswell debris - the single act that restarted the Roswell case after thirty years of silence and made him, as he put it, the first civilian to document the site. He fed Marcel to William Moore and Charles Berlitz, whose 1980 'The Roswell Incident' made the case public. From 1984 he was the principal defender of the Majestic 12 documents received by Moore and Jaime Shandera, publishing 'Top Secret/Majic' in 1996 and maintaining that no substantive grounds existed for dismissing the authenticity of the core documents - a position that split him permanently from Randle, Klass and much of the field. He was also the first to demonstrate that some MJ-12 papers were provably faked, showing that a purported 17 February 1948 Hillenkoetter-to-Truman memo was an emulation of a Marshall-to-Roosevelt letter reproduced in 'The American MAGIC'. He testified in writing to a House committee in 1968, appeared twice at the United Nations, and donated his research files to the Provincial Archives of New Brunswick shortly before his death.
people.tierRationale: He is the causal link between the Roswell witness chain and the public record: without his 1978 contact with Jesse Marcel Sr. there is no modern Roswell literature. His MJ-12 advocacy is the field's largest single unresolved evidentiary dispute.

people.label: Kevin D. Randle
people.sub: Lt Col (ret.), USAF/Army/Iowa NG intelligence officer; Roswell author
people.narrative: Kevin Douglas Randle (born 4 June 1949) is the closest thing the retrieval literature has to an internal auditor with a security background. He flew UH-1s with the 116th and 187th Assault Helicopter Companies in Vietnam, served in the Air Force as a public affairs officer, general's aide and intelligence officer, completed Air Force Reserve service as a captain and director of intelligence for an airlift group, then joined the Iowa National Guard as an intelligence officer after 11 September 2001, deploying with the 234th Signal Battalion to Baghdad International Airport in June 2003 and retiring as a lieutenant colonel in 2009. With Donald R. Schmitt he wrote 'UFO Crash at Roswell' (1991) and 'The Truth About the UFO Crash at Roswell' (1994), the two books that drove Roswell into congressional attention and produced the Air Force counter-reports. Randle is important to this board precisely because he moved against the current: he demolished the Majestic 12 documents in 'Conclusions on Operation Majestic Twelve' (1994) and 'Case MJ-12' (2002) while Friedman defended them, he withdrew his and Schmitt's support for witnesses who did not hold up, and he later told Skeptical Inquirer's Robert Sheaffer that he sets a very high bar for evidence, that most abductees are describing sleep paralysis, and eventually that he was 'no longer sure what actually happened' at Roswell and that the case for extraterrestrial involvement 'is no longer robust.' He also wrote 'Project Moon Dust' (1999), 'A History of UFO Crashes' (1995) and 'Crash: When UFOs Fall From the Sky' (2010), which is the field's most systematic case-by-case survey.

people.label: Maj. Jesse A. Marcel Sr.
people.sub: Air intelligence officer, 509th Bomb Group, Roswell AAF, 1947
people.narrative: Jesse Antoine Marcel Sr. (27 May 1907 - 23 June 1986) is the first link in the entire modern retrieval witness chain, and the only one whose custody of the material is documented in a contemporaneous 1947 record rather than in later testimony. Commissioned in the Army Air Forces in April 1942, trained as a combat photo interpreter and intelligence officer at Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, he served with 5th Bomber Command in the Southwest Pacific, flew combat missions, won two Air Medals and the Bronze Star, and was attached to the 509th Composite Group for Operation Crossroads at Bikini in 1946, drawing letters of commendation from Brig. Gen. Roger M. Ramey and Maj. Gen. W. E. Kepner. On 7 July 1947 he and CIC agent Lt. Col. Sheridan Cavitt drove out with rancher Mac Brazel to the debris field on the Foster ranch near Corona and loaded material into a vehicle; the 8 July Roswell Army Air Field press release naming him as the responsible officer went worldwide, and he flew the debris to Fort Worth where Ramey held the press conference that replaced the disc with a weather balloon and photographed Marcel kneeling beside it. He said nothing publicly for thirty-one years. In February 1978 Stanton Friedman was put in touch with him in Baton Rouge, and Marcel - then a retired lieutenant colonel - stated that the balloon story was a cover, that the material he handled was not of this earth, and that the debris photographed at Fort Worth was not the debris he brought in. Everything downstream in this domain runs through that interview: Berlitz and Moore's 1980 book, Randle and Schmitt, Friedman's own MJ-12 turn, and the 1994-1997 Air Force counter-reports were all responses to a retired intelligence major changing his story.
affiliations: 509th Composite Group / 509th Bomb Group, Roswell AAF
people.tierRationale: The only Roswell figure whose physical handling of the recovered material is attested in a same-week official document (the RAAF press release naming him) as well as in his own later testimony. Custody proximity 3.

people.label: Dr. Jesse A. Marcel Jr.
people.sub: Physician; USN/Army flight surgeon; son of Maj. Jesse Marcel Sr.; child witness to the debris
people.narrative: Jesse A. Marcel Jr. was eleven years old in July 1947 when his father woke him in the middle of the night at their Roswell house and spread pieces of the recovered debris on the kitchen floor. He spent his adult life as a physician - an ear, nose and throat surgeon, a Navy flight surgeon and later an Army National Guard flight surgeon who deployed to Iraq in his late sixties - and he gave the same account of that night, in substantially the same words, for over thirty years: metallic foil that would not stay creased, small structural beams, and on one beam a row of embossed symbols he consistently described as purple-violet geometric figures resembling nothing he could read. He signed a sworn affidavit for the Fund for UFO Research in the early 1990s, testified in the 2001 Disclosure Project event, submitted to hypnosis to recover further detail, and co-wrote 'The Roswell Legacy' (2009) with Linda Marcel. His evidentiary value is specific and limited, and stating the limit is what makes it usable: he is a first-hand witness to material in his father's hands, not to a craft, not to bodies, and not to a recovery operation. He is also the field's most stable witness - the standard criticism of Roswell testimony is drift and elaboration, and Marcel Jr.'s account demonstrably did neither across decades of retelling under adversarial questioning.

people.label: 1st Lt. Walter G. Haut
people.sub: Public information officer, 509th Bomb Group; author of the 8 July 1947 'flying disc' press release
people.narrative: Walter G. Haut (3 June 1922 - 15 December 2005) wrote the sentence that started all of it. A bombardier who flew thirty-five missions against Japan and dropped instrument packages at the Bikini tests in 1946, he became public information officer for the 509th Bomb Group at Roswell Army Air Field, and on 8 July 1947 base commander Col. William H. Blanchard - a close personal friend - told him to write and distribute a release stating the field had come into possession of a flying disc. He did, and the story went round the world before Fort Worth retracted it the same day. Haut's own testimony evolved in a documented, dateable sequence that this board records in full because the sequence is the evidence. In 1980's 'The Roswell Incident' he is explicitly 'not a witness.' In 1979 and again in a March 1989 interview he said he knew nothing of what was recovered and had been refused when he asked to see it. In a sworn affidavit signed 14 May 1993 he added that Blanchard must have seen the material himself and that neither Blanchard nor Marcel could have mistaken it for a weather balloon. Then, in December 2002, Donald Schmitt composed and emailed a further affidavit which Haut signed at the International UFO Museum in front of his daughter Julie Shuster and a notary, on the agreement that it would not be released until after his death; it asserts first-hand sight of a craft and bodies. Haut died in 2005 and the document was published by Carey and Schmitt in 'Witness to Roswell' (2007). A witness whose claims escalate monotonically over twenty-two years, with the largest escalation drafted by his interviewer and embargoed until he could not be cross-examined, is a specific kind of evidence, and this board grades it as such.

people.label: W. Glenn Dennis
people.sub: Mortician, Ballard Funeral Home, Roswell, 1947; 'missing nurse' witness
people.narrative: Glenn Dennis (24 March 1925 - 28 April 2015) was a 22-year-old embalmer at the Ballard Funeral Home, which held the mortuary contract with Roswell Army Air Field, when he says he received calls from the base mortuary officer in July 1947 asking about child-sized hermetically sealed caskets and about preserving bodies exposed to the elements. He came to researchers' attention in 1994 after telephoning an Unsolved Mysteries tip line, and became for a time the case's star witness on the strength of a story about being ejected from the base hospital and meeting a nurse who described small non-human autopsies. The story collapsed under exactly the kind of audit that this board treats as decisive. The Air Force's 1997 report obtained the certified daily morning reports of the 427th AAF Base Unit Squadron 'M', the unit to which all Roswell AAF medical personnel were assigned, and established that the Army Nurse Corps strength at the field in July 1947 was five nurses; none was transferred on 8 or 9 July, none was sent overseas and none was killed in a plane crash; the one nurse reassigned went to Fort Worth AAF on 23 July by normal rotation. The National Personnel Records Center found no record that a 'Naomi Maria Selff' had ever served in any branch of the US armed forces. Dennis later told Thomas Carey and Donald Schmitt that he had knowingly given them a false name, and they wrote in 'Witness to Roswell' that he 'must technically stand impeached as a witness.' What survives is narrow and worth keeping: independent people say Dennis told them about the child-sized casket calls and the hospital confrontation long before Roswell was a commercial subject.

people.label: James Ragsdale
people.sub: Claimed civilian eyewitness to a crash site north of Roswell
people.narrative: James Ragsdale came forward in the 1990s claiming that he and a companion had been camping north of Roswell in July 1947 and had seen a crashed craft and bodies, with a military recovery arriving afterwards. He gave a sworn statement and a videotaped deathbed account, and Randle and Schmitt used him to anchor the impact site in 'The Truth About the UFO Crash at Roswell' (1994). Two things about Ragsdale are load-bearing and both cut against the case. First, his account moved: the location he gave shifted materially between tellings, in a way that tracked which impact site the researchers then favoured. Second, and more usefully, the Air Force's 1997 report quotes him saying of the objects at the site, 'They were using dummies in those damned things' - the witness himself volunteering the anthropomorphic dummy reading that the Air Force went on to adopt as its explanation. The Air Force notes he lived and worked around Roswell, Artesia and Carlsbad in the period when Alderson Laboratories anthropomorphic dummies were being dropped by high-altitude balloon and recovered by uniformed teams, and concludes he probably described one or more of nine documented dummy recoveries near there.
people.tierRationale: Tier C. Named but self-contradicting witness, retained because his own quoted words are the sharpest illustration of the dummy-recovery competing explanation.

people.label: Grady L. 'Barney' Barnett
people.sub: Soil Conservation Service engineer; original claimed Plains of San Agustin eyewitness
people.narrative: Grady L. 'Barney' Barnett was a soil conservation engineer who travelled widely in New Mexico and who, according to friends, described coming upon a crashed disc and small bodies in open country, with an archaeological field party present, before military personnel arrived and cleared everyone out. Barnett died in 1969, years before anyone thought to record him, and every version of his account reaching the literature is second-hand, given by Vern Maltais and Alice Knight decades later - Knight on camera saying flatly, 'I don't recall the date.' The account entered the record through Berlitz and Moore's 'The Roswell Incident' (1980) and became the load-bearing support for a second, separate 1947 crash on the Plains of San Agustin, 175 miles northwest of Roswell. The Air Force's 1997 report offers a specific and testable alternative: that Maltais and Knight, thirty-plus years on, confused the Plains of San Agustin with San Agustin Pass or San Agustin Peak in the San Agustin Mountains, immediately outside White Sands Missile Range and the Jornada Test Range, where numerous anthropomorphic dummy balloon flights terminated and were recovered by military teams. Barnett is the clearest case in the whole domain of an account that cannot be graded above tier 3 by construction: the only first-hand witness died before being interviewed.
people.tierRationale: Tier C. The originating witness for an entire claimed crash site who was never interviewed by any researcher. Included because the San Agustin strand cannot be discussed without him.

people.label: Gerald Anderson
people.sub: Claimed first-hand child witness, Plains of San Agustin, 1947
people.narrative: Gerald Anderson came forward in 1990, after a television broadcast, claiming that as a five-year-old he had been rockhounding with his family on the Plains of San Agustin in July 1947 and had walked up to a crashed disc with dead and one living occupant. He was the only claimed first-hand witness to the San Agustin site and was accordingly promoted hard by Stanton Friedman and Don Berliner in 'Crash at Corona' (1992). The case against him was made not by the Air Force but by other ufologists: Mark Rodeghier of CUFOS and Fred Whiting of the Fund for UFO Research produced a joint report, 'The Plains of San Agustin Controversy', which established among other things that a telephone bill Anderson submitted as corroboration had been altered. His own quoted words in the Air Force's 1997 report - 'I thought they were plastic dolls' - and his descriptions of the recovery procedures were read by the Air Force as accurate reporting of an anthropomorphic dummy balloon launch and recovery, of which numerous examples were flown and recovered in the region. Anderson matters to this board as the field's most instructive self-correction: two civilian research organisations audited their own star witness and published the result against interest.

people.label: Frank Scully
people.sub: Variety columnist; author, 'Behind the Flying Saucers' (1950)
people.narrative: Francis Joseph Xavier Scully (28 April 1892 - 23 June 1964), a Variety columnist and humorist, wrote the first crashed-saucer book. Two 1949 Variety columns and then 'Behind the Flying Saucers' (Henry Holt, 1950) told readers that in March 1948 a 99-foot disc containing sixteen small humanoid bodies had come down in Hart Canyon twelve miles northeast of Aztec, New Mexico, had been taken by the military for secret research, ran on magnetic principles, came from Venus, and had every dimension divisible by nine. Scully's named sources were Silas M. Newton and a scientist he described as having 'more degrees than a thermometer' - later identified as Leo A. Gebauer. The book was a bestseller and it set the template: crash, bodies, immediate military cordon, exotic material, total official silence. San Francisco Chronicle reporter J. P. Cahn published exposures in True magazine in 1952 and 1956 showing Newton and Gebauer were confidence men selling 'doodlebug' oil-finding devices they claimed were built on recovered alien technology; a metal sample they supplied Cahn was ordinary aluminium; and in 1953 both were convicted of fraud after millionaire Herman Flader pressed charges. Scully is on this board as the origin of the crash-retrieval genre and as the reason the genre carried a fraud provenance from its first page - a provenance that Leonard Stringfield, Ryan Wood and the Aztec revivalists have each had to argue around rather than through.
people.tierRationale: Tier B: the first author of a crash-retrieval book, whose sources were criminally convicted for the fraud that produced the story. Central to the domain's provenance problem.

people.label: Dr. Robert M. Wood
people.sub: PhD physics; 43 years at McDonnell Douglas; co-principal, The Majestic Documents
people.narrative: Robert M. Wood is the aerospace-industry end of the retrieval literature. He holds a doctorate in physics and spent forty-three years at McDonnell Douglas, where he managed advanced propulsion and effects research - including, on his own account, a company-funded study in the late 1960s and early 1970s into whether UFO field-propulsion effects could be replicated. That places him in the same institutional category as Stanton Friedman: a cleared contractor engineer who concluded from the inside that a compartmented programme was plausible. With his son Ryan S. Wood he built The Majestic Documents project, an online archive at majesticdocuments.com which since 1999 has collected, published, catalogued and applied a stated authenticity-rating scheme to the MJ-12 and related leaked-document corpus - including the Special Operations Manual SOM1-01, the 'Interplanetary Phenomenon Unit' material, and the Air Accident Report papers. The project's importance to this board is methodological rather than evidentiary: Wood insisted on treating the documents as forensic objects - typeface, paper, watermark, ink, format, security-marking convention and internal administrative plausibility - rather than as scripture, and published the ratings. Whether one accepts the conclusions, the framework is the only sustained forensic protocol ever applied to the leaked-document corpus, and no agency has ever published a competing analysis.

people.label: Ryan S. Wood
people.sub: Author, 'Majic Eyes Only: Earth's Encounters with Extraterrestrial Technology' (2005); co-principal, The Majestic Documents
people.narrative: Ryan S. Wood did the thing the retrieval field had never done: he built a catalogue. 'Majic Eyes Only: Earth's Encounters with Extraterrestrial Technology' (2005) assembles the claimed crash-retrieval events into a single indexed database, each entry given a date, a location, a source trail and a numerical credibility weighting, running from the 1940s to the modern era and totalling seventy-plus events. The book is the direct methodological descendant of Stringfield's Status Reports and of Kevin Randle's 'A History of UFO Crashes', but where Stringfield presented anonymised narratives and Randle presented case essays, Wood presented rows in a table with a scoring column - which is what makes it usable and what makes it attackable. Wood also co-runs The Majestic Documents archive with his father Robert M. Wood and organises the annual UFO Crash Retrieval Conference series, which functioned through the 2000s as the field's clearing house for new retrieval claims. For this board, 'Majic Eyes Only' is best treated as the field's index rather than as its evidence: it is where you go to find out that a claim exists and who first made it, not to find out whether it is true.

people.label: Richard M. Dolan
people.sub: Historian; author, 'UFOs and the National Security State' vols. I-II
people.narrative: Richard M. Dolan is the field's historian rather than its investigator, and that distinction is the point. Trained in history - he studied at Alfred University and Oxford and was a Rhodes Scholar finalist, with graduate work at the University of Rochester on Cold War strategy and the national security state - he wrote 'UFOs and the National Security State: Chronology of a Cover-Up, 1941-1973' (2002) and 'UFOs and the National Security State: The Cover-Up Exposed, 1973-1991' (2009). The two volumes did something the crash-retrieval literature had never done: they placed the UFO record inside the documented institutional history of American secrecy - the National Security Act of 1947, the special access programme structure, the intelligence reorganisations, contractor black programmes - and argued that the concealment is a normal output of that machinery rather than an exotic conspiracy requiring exotic explanation. Dolan coined and popularised the 'breakaway civilisation' formulation for a technologically self-sustaining compartment operating outside public accountability. He hosts The Richard Dolan Show, has published on the Wilson-Davis memorandum and on the 2020-2023 disclosure sequence, and is one of the small number of researchers whose framing survived the transition from the 1990s literature to the post-2017 congressional era intact - because it was built on the secrecy architecture, which is documented, rather than on witness testimony, which is not.
people.tierRationale: Tier A: author of the standard scholarly chronology of the domain, and the researcher whose analytical frame - concealment as a product of documented SAP architecture - is the one this board's premise is built on.

people.label: Grant Cameron
people.sub: Canadian researcher; presidential UFO briefings; presidentialufo.com
people.narrative: Grant Cameron works the narrowest and most institutionally checkable question in the field: what have presidents been told, when, and by whom. Beginning from the 1975 Charlie Red Star sightings in Carman, Manitoba, he shifted in the 1980s to documentary research on the executive branch, filing FOIA requests with presidential libraries and the White House and assembling the presidentialufo.com archive of correspondence, memoranda and staff records touching UFOs from Truman onwards. His long-running work on the Clinton administration - the Rockefeller Initiative, Webster Hubbell's memoir statement that Clinton asked him to find out about UFOs, and John Podesta's role - is the strand that connects most directly to the modern disclosure fight, since Podesta went on to chair the Sci Fi Channel's Coalition for Freedom of Information and to press for NASA and Air Force record releases. Cameron's method is the opposite of the witness-driven literature: he requests paper from institutions that have to log the request, and publishes what comes back including the null returns. That makes his output unusually gradeable, and it is why he sits on this board despite advancing interpretive claims about consciousness and contact that are not gradeable at all.
people.tierRationale: Tier B: a FOIA-first researcher whose subject matter - executive-branch knowledge - is exactly the question this board exists to answer, and whose returns are institutionally logged and therefore auditable.

people.label: Robert L. Hastings
people.sub: Researcher, UFO incursions at US nuclear weapons sites; author, 'UFOs and Nukes'
people.narrative: Robert Hastings has spent more than forty years doing one thing: locating and interviewing US Air Force personnel who were present at nuclear weapons sites during unexplained aerial incursions, and pairing their testimony with declassified documents obtained under FOIA. He states he has interviewed over 150 military veterans involved in such incidents at missile sites, weapons storage facilities and bomb test ranges, and he has published the underlying paper - FBI memoranda on Los Alamos in December 1948 and on Los Alamos and Sandia in August 1950, F. E. Warren AFB documents from 1 August 1965, Minot AFB material from 1966, the 17 March 1967 Air Force teletype reporting loss of strategic alert at Malmstrom, and 1975 Malmstrom documents - alongside signed witness affidavits. On 27 September 2010 he hosted the UFO-Nukes Connection press conference at the National Press Club in Washington DC, at which seven US Air Force veterans described incursions at nuclear weapons sites; CNN streamed the event live. That event is the single most important item in this section of the board, because it converted a body of anonymous or semi-anonymous claims into named, on-the-record testimony from identifiable former officers with signed affidavits on file - which is the difference between tier 3 and tier 2. His book 'UFOs and Nukes: Extraordinary Encounters at Nuclear Weapons Sites' is in a revised second edition of 580 pages, and his documentary 'UFOs and Nukes: The Secret Link Revealed' followed. people.label: Capt. Robert L. Salas
people.sub: USAF Academy graduate; Minuteman missile launch officer, 341st SMW, Malmstrom AFB, March 1967
people.narrative: Robert L. Salas is the named officer at the centre of the Malmstrom March 1967 missile shutdown claim. A US Air Force Academy graduate with a master's in aerospace engineering from the Air Force Institute of Technology, he served seven years on active duty as an ICBM launch controller and missile propulsion engineer, resigned his commission in 1971, worked at Martin Marietta and Rockwell International, then spent two decades at the Federal Aviation Administration to about 1995. He first went on the record in a 1996 interview with the Great Falls Tribune: while on duty in a launch control capsule at Malmstrom he took a call from a topside Air Force security police officer reporting a glowing red object hovering over the front gate, and within moments the missiles in his flight went off alert status one after another. He has repeated the account in a signed affidavit held by Robert Hastings, in his books 'Faded Giant' (2005, with James Klotz) and 'Unidentified' (2014), at the 27 September 2010 National Press Club event, and in the 2025 documentary 'The Age of Disclosure'. His most important corroboration is a letter from his commander, Col. Frederick Meiwald, dated 1 October 1996, published in facsimile by Hastings. Salas is also the case where this board's grading discipline bites hardest in both directions: the underlying fact that a Malmstrom flight of ten Minuteman missiles went off alert in March 1967 is documented in Air Force paper, while the causal attribution to an aerial object is testimony, and a competing engineering explanation - a nearby electromagnetic pulse simulator test - has been advanced against it.
people.tierRationale: Tier A: a named, commissioned, on-the-record officer with a signed affidavit, a corroborating letter from his own commander, and a documented underlying missile-shutdown event. The disputed element is causation, not occurrence.

people.sub: Investigative journalist; FOIA plaintiff in Kean v. NASA; co-author of the 2017 NYT AATIP story
people.narrative: Leslie Kean is the person in this domain who took the government to court and won a search. On 31 January 2003 she filed a FOIA request with NASA for records referring to Kecksburg, the incident of 9 December 1965, the 'Fragology Files' for 1962-1967, Richard M. Schulherr, Project Moon Dust and Cosmos 96. NASA answered 'no records' on 11 April 2003. She appealed; NASA's Associate Deputy Administrator James Jennings granted the appeal on 18 June 2003 and promised an expedited agency-wide search; NASA then failed to act on its own letter, a failure the court later attributed to poor tracking and the relocation of the FOIA office. On 15 October 2003 she notified NASA she intended to sue, and on 9 December 2003 - thirty-eight years to the day after Kecksburg - she filed Kean v. National Aeronautics and Space Administration, Civil Action No. 03-2509 (EGS), in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, represented by Lobel, Novins & Lamont. Judge Emmet G. Sullivan held a hearing on 20 March 2007 and on 27 March 2007 issued a memorandum opinion finding that NASA had not met its burden of showing its searches were adequate, denying the agency summary judgment on the search question and ordering the parties to propose search and documentation procedures that would create a proper record. NASA settled in part on 16 October 2007 and searched under court supervision, filing joint status reports every sixty days until the case was dismissed on 24 August 2009. Kean went on to write 'UFOs: Generals, Pilots and Government Officials Go on the Record' (2010) and, with Ralph Blumenthal and Helene Cooper, the 16 December 2017 New York Times story that revealed AATIP.

people.label: Col. Richard L. Weaver
people.sub: Director, Security and Special Program Oversight, Office of the Secretary of the Air Force
people.narrative: Col. Richard L. Weaver ran the Air Force's official answer to Roswell, and his job title is the most interesting fact about him. He was Director of Security and Special Program Oversight in the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force - that is, the officer responsible for oversight of Air Force special access programmes - and it was that office, not a historical or public affairs office, that the Secretary tasked to respond to the General Accounting Office inquiry initiated by Rep. Steven H. Schiff. Weaver and 1st Lt. James McAndrew produced the July 1994 report to the Secretary of the Air Force, published in 1995 by the Government Printing Office as 'The Roswell Report: Fact Versus Fiction in the New Mexico Desert'. Its conclusion was Project Mogul: the classified balloon-borne acoustic programme flown from Alamogordo Army Air Field to detect Soviet nuclear tests, whose flight from 4 June 1947 was lost within seventeen miles of the Foster ranch. Weaver's report also states something operationally significant that is rarely quoted: at the express written direction of the Secretary of the Air Force, former and retired Air Force members and civilian contract scientists were released from any nondisclosure obligations they might have entered into on the relevant past classified activities, so that they could speak freely. This board records Weaver as an oversight-cluster node with A=3 not because he asserts access to a recovery programme - he denies one exists - but because the Secretary routed the inquiry to the SAP oversight directorate, which is a fact about where the Air Force believed the answer would have to be looked for.
affiliations: Office of the Secretary of the Air Force, Director of Security and Special Program Oversight
people.tierRationale: Tier A. Author of the United States government's principal official denial in this domain, written from the special access programme oversight desk. A denial from that desk is a first-order artifact.

people.label: Capt. James McAndrew
people.sub: USAF intelligence officer; author, 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed' (1997)
people.narrative: James McAndrew, born 1963, was the junior officer who did the archival work on both Air Force Roswell reports and the sole named author of the second. As a first lieutenant he wrote Attachment 32 of the 1995 report - the Project Mogul synopsis that carries the Air Force's whole 1947 explanation. He then produced 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed' (1997), published by Headquarters United States Air Force through the Government Printing Office, a 231-page volume addressing the claims of alien bodies that the 1994-1995 report had not covered. His method is the reason that book matters on this board irrespective of whether one accepts its conclusion: rather than asserting a denial he went to the certified records - the 427th Army Air Forces Base Unit Squadron 'M' morning reports, the National Personnel Records Center, aircraft accident files, Alderson Laboratories dummy launch and recovery logs - and printed the documents, the anthropomorphic dummy launch and landing locations at Appendix A, the sworn witness statements of ten named Air Force personnel at Appendix B including Col. Joseph W. Kittinger Jr., and full interview transcripts of Gerald Anderson, Glenn Dennis, Alice Knight, Vern Maltais and James Ragsdale at Appendix C. In other words the government's denial published its own primary sources and named its own witnesses, which is the standard against which every claim on this board should be measured, including the claims this board finds persuasive.

people.tierRationale: Tier A. Sole author of the official counter-report that is the most heavily documented single artifact in the Roswell record, on either side.

people.label: William L. Moore
people.sub: Co-author, 'The Roswell Incident' (1980); first recipient of the MJ-12 film; self-confessed conduit for AFOSI disinformation
people.narrative: William L. Moore wrote the book that made Roswell a public case and then, nine years later, told a room full of ufologists that he had been working with Air Force counterintelligence. With Charles Berlitz he published 'The Roswell Incident' (Grosset & Dunlap, 1980), built on Stanton Friedman's 1978 contact with Jesse Marcel Sr. and on the second-hand Barney Barnett material, and it established the modern case. In December 1984 he and Jaime Shandera received in the post a roll of undeveloped 35mm film containing the Eisenhower Briefing Document and the Truman-Forrestal memorandum - the origin of the entire MJ-12 corpus that Friedman then spent a decade defending and Randle a decade attacking. At the 1989 MUFON symposium in Las Vegas, Moore stated publicly that from about 1980 he had cooperated with personnel of the Air Force Office of Special Investigations, and that he had knowingly passed disinformation to the Albuquerque physicist and businessman Paul Bennewitz, whose mental health collapsed under it. That admission is the single most consequential statement ever made by a researcher in this field, and this board treats it structurally rather than moralistically: it establishes, on the admission of the participant, that a US counterintelligence element used a civilian UFO researcher as a delivery channel for fabricated material into the UFO community. Any document, witness or claim entering the record through that channel between roughly 1980 and 1989 - and the MJ-12 papers arrived in the middle of it - carries a provenance problem that cannot be argued away.
affiliations: Co-author with Charles Berlitz, 'The Roswell Incident' (1980)
people.tierRationale: Tier B: author of the founding Roswell book and, by his own public admission, a conduit for official disinformation. He is the domain's provenance hazard made explicit.

people.label: John F. Schuessler
people.sub: NASA/McDonnell Douglas aerospace engineer; MUFON International Director 2000-2006; Cash-Landrum investigator
people.narrative: John F. Schuessler is the reason the Cash-Landrum case has a documentary record at all. An aerospace engineer working on NASA manned spaceflight programmes through McDonnell Douglas, he was the person Vickie Landrum was steered to when she telephoned NASA in early 1981, and with his group Project VISIT he began investigating within weeks: a taped interview at Parkway Hospital in early February 1981, an on-site investigation on 28 February 1981, and a 35-page preliminary report to MUFON dated 4 March 1981. He then spent seventeen years accumulating the witnesses' medical records, radiological survey results, physician correspondence and legal papers, publishing them in 'The Cash-Landrum UFO Incident' (1998) - which is why sceptics such as Gary Posner and Brian Dunning have been able to argue against the case using Schuessler's own printed medical documentation. He served as MUFON International Director from 2000 to 2006. Schuessler is the type specimen of the credentialled contractor-engineer investigator, the same category as Robert M. Wood and Stanton Friedman, and his significance for this board is that he built the only major UFO case file assembled to something approaching a medico-legal standard - and that the case still failed in federal court, on evidence.

people.label: Betty Cash

people.narrative: Betty Cash was fifty-one on the night of 29 December 1980 when, with Vickie Landrum and seven-year-old Colby Landrum, she stopped her car on a two-lane road near Huffman, Texas, in front of what all three described as an intensely bright object expelling flame, followed by a formation of tandem-rotor helicopters they counted at around twenty-three. She stood outside the car longest and was injured worst: hospitalised from 2 January 1981, with blistering, hair loss and eye symptoms, later treated for breast cancer. She became the lead named plaintiff in Betty Cash, Vickie Landrum and Colby Landrum v. United States of America, Civil Action No. H-84-348, filed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas, Houston Division, on 18 January 1984 under the Federal Tort Claims Act, 28 U.S.C. 1346(b) and 2671 et seq. Her attorney in charge was Peter A. Gersten of Gagliardi, Torpes & Gersten, Tarrytown, New York, with William C. Shead as local co-counsel. On 21 August 1986 Judge Ross N. Sterling granted the government's motion and entered an Order of Dismissal under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 12(b)(1), 12(b)(6) and 56. This board records Cash at tier A not because the object is identified - it is not - but because she is the only UFO witness in the United States to have forced the government to appear in a federal court and answer, on the record, whether an object and aircraft of that description were its own.

people.label: Stan Gordon
people.sub: Pennsylvania field researcher; principal investigator of the 1965 Kecksburg incident
people.narrative: Stan Gordon is the field researcher who kept Kecksburg alive for four decades until it reached a federal courtroom. A western Pennsylvania investigator who was a teenager in Greensburg when the fireball came down on 9 December 1965, he spent the following decades locating and interviewing local witnesses - residents who described a military and state police cordon thrown around the woods, a flatbed truck leaving the site carrying something acorn-shaped and about the size of a Volkswagen, and men in unmarked vehicles - while the official position remained that searchers found absolutely nothing. His witness pool supplied the 1990 Unsolved Mysteries episode, the 2003 Sci Fi Channel documentary 'The New Roswell: Kecksburg Exposed', and, indirectly, the evidentiary basis for Leslie Kean's 2003 FOIA request and lawsuit against NASA. Gordon's work is the standard illustration of the retrieval literature's characteristic profile: a large, internally consistent body of local first-hand testimony describing a recovery operation, and no document. The Kean litigation was the attempt to close that gap by force of law, and it produced a federal finding that NASA's searches were inadequate and sworn testimony that two boxes of records from the period were missing - not the object, but the paper trail of its absence.
affiliations: Pennsylvania Association for the Study of the Unexplained (PASU), founder

entities.label: UFO Crash/Retrieval Status Reports I-VII (Stringfield, 1978-1994)
entities.sub: Seven-part self-published monograph series, 1978-1994
entities.desc: The seven UFO Crash/Retrieval Status Reports written by Leonard H. Stringfield between 1978 and 1994 are the founding corpus of the crash-retrieval literature and the reason the subject exists as a research field rather than as folklore. Status Report I is 'Retrievals of the Third Kind: A Case Study of Alleged UFOs and Occupants in Military Custody', delivered as a paper at the ninth annual MUFON Symposium in Dayton, Ohio on 29 July 1978 (revised 20 July 1978) and published in Flying Saucer Review; it grew out of the informant response to Stringfield's 1977 Doubleday book 'Situation Red, The UFO Siege'. Status Report II, 'The UFO Crash/Retrieval Syndrome: New Sources, New Data', is dated January 1980 and was published by MUFON; it introduced the letter-number case coding (Cases A-1 onward, Items B-1 onward) that structures the whole series, and included the first Del Rio and Wright-Patterson entries. Status Report III, 'Amassing the Evidence' (1982), carried endorsements from Dr. Peter Rank, Chief of Radiology at Methodist Hospital, and Richard H. Hall, former Assistant Director of NICAP and editor of the MUFON UFO Journal, and printed a consolidated chronology of every case reported in Status Report II - the field's first tabulated retrieval index. Status Report IV, 'The Fatal Encounter at Ft. Dix-McGuire: A Case Study' (June 1985), is a single-case monograph on an alleged 18 January 1978 incident at McGuire AFB and Fort Dix, developed from a USAF Security Police sergeant who had first appeared as Case A3 in Report III, and opens with a prologue titled 'The Burden of Proof' in which Stringfield states that public research does not possess proof and that affidavits, leaked documents and photographs are not proof. Status Report V, 'Is the Coverup Lid Lifting?' (January 1989), surveys Roswell, Aztec, Kingman, El Yunque and Brown County, Ohio, and argues that confirming any single retrieval would compel eventual sharing of alien propulsion and materials technology. Status Report VI, 'The Inner Sanctum' (July 1991), was self-published from 4412 Grove Avenue, Cincinnati, edited by Richard Hall and typed by Chris Coffey, and opens with the Humpty Dumpty verse from Through the Looking Glass. Status Report VII, 'Search for Proof in a Hall of Mirrors' (February 1994), acknowledges funding from the Fund for UFO Research and cooperation from MUFON, CUFOS and the Mid-Ohio Research Associates, opens with Walter Scott's 'I cannot tell how the truth may be; I say the tale as 'twas told to me', and closes the series ten months before Stringfield's death with a Roswell crash/retrieval update noting a source's placement of the site north of Roswell rather than on the Plains of San Augustin. The series' method - anonymous sources behind letter-number codes - is simultaneously the reason the material exists and the reason almost none of it can be graded above tier 2.

entities.label: The Roswell Report: Fact Versus Fiction in the New Mexico Desert (1995)
entities.sub: Office of the Secretary of the Air Force report to GAO; GPO, 1995
entities.desc: The first of the two official Air Force Roswell reports, written by Col. Richard L. Weaver, Director of Security and Special Program Oversight in the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force, with 1st Lt. James McAndrew. It was produced to answer Rep. Steven H. Schiff's inquiry as routed through the General Accounting Office, delivered to the Secretary of the Air Force and to GAO in July 1994, and published by the Government Printing Office in 1995. Its operative conclusion is that the July 1947 debris came from Project Mogul, the top-priority classified balloon-borne acoustic programme flown from Alamogordo Army Air Field to detect Soviet nuclear tests, described in McAndrew's Attachment 32. The published version duplicates the report delivered to the Secretary and GAO with the addition of a photograph section. The document's evidentiary character is unusual and this board treats it accordingly: it is a denial, and it is also a primary record. It establishes on the government's own signature that a classified programme was flying from Alamogordo in June-July 1947 whose existence had been concealed for forty-seven years, that the Secretary of the Air Force issued a written direction releasing former airmen and contract scientists from nondisclosure obligations so they could speak, and that the inquiry was assigned to the special access programme oversight directorate rather than to a historical office. Every one of those three facts is a fact about the concealment architecture, whatever one concludes about the balloon.

entities.label: The Roswell Report: Case Closed (1997)
entities.sub: HQ USAF / GPO, by Capt. James McAndrew; 231 pp.
entities.desc: The second and more consequential official Air Force report, authored by James McAndrew and published by Headquarters United States Air Force through the Government Printing Office in 1997, addressing the alien-bodies claims that the 1994-1995 report had not covered. Its four stated conclusions are that Air Force activities spanning many years were consolidated into two or three days in July 1947; that the 'aliens' were probably anthropomorphic test dummies carried aloft by high-altitude balloons; that the 'unusual' military activity in the desert was balloon launch and recovery, with the units that always arrived shortly after a crash being accurate descriptions of dummy-recovery teams; and that the Roswell Army Air Field hospital bodies claims most likely combine a 1956 KC-97 crash killing eleven airmen with a 1959 manned balloon mishap injuring two pilots. The report also asserts flatly that 'the claims of bodies only became part of the Roswell Incident after 1978'. What makes it a first-order artifact rather than a press release is what it printed: anthropomorphic dummy launch and landing locations at Appendix A; sworn witness statements from ten named Air Force personnel at Appendix B including Col. Joseph W. Kittinger Jr., Col. Dan D. Fulgham, Bernard D. Gildenberg and Lt. Col. Raymond A. Madson; and full interview transcripts of five pro-UFO witnesses at Appendix C - Gerald Anderson, Glenn Dennis, Alice Knight, Vern Maltais and James Ragsdale, the Dennis interview supplied by its interviewer Karl T. Pflock. Section 2.1 is the most forensically detailed passage the US government has ever published on a UFO claim: it works the 427th AAF Base Unit Squadron 'M' morning reports and the National Personnel Records Center holdings to establish that Glenn Dennis's 'Naomi Maria Selff' never existed and to identify 1st Lt. Eileen M. Fanton as matching every other particular of his description.

claims.text: The report identifies its four conclusions as consolidation of many years of Air Force activity into July 1947; anthropomorphic test dummies as the 'aliens'; high-altitude balloon launch and recovery as the 'unusual' military activity; and a 1956 KC-97 accident plus a 1959 manned balloon mishap as the source of the hospital bodies accounts.

entities.label: Kean v. NASA, No. 1:03-cv-02509 (D.D.C.)
entities.sub: Federal FOIA litigation over the Kecksburg records, 2003-2009
entities.desc: The only federal court case in which a US agency has been held to have failed its search obligations on UFO-related records. Leslie Kean, represented by Lobel, Novins & Lamont (Martin Lobel, Lee Ellen Helfrich), sued the National Aeronautics and Space Administration on 9 December 2003 in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia over NASA's handling of her 31 January 2003 FOIA request for records referring to Kecksburg, the 9 December 1965 incident, the 'Fragology Files' for 1962-1967, Richard M. Schulherr, Project Moon Dust and Cosmos 96. The case was assigned to Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, cause code '05:552 Freedom of Information Act', PACER case ID 106063. NASA ran four searches. The court's 27 March 2007 memorandum opinion records that 'plaintiff contends, and indeed NASA admits, that NASA's first two searches for responsive documents were inadequate', traces how a granted administrative appeal signed by Associate Deputy Administrator James Jennings on 18 June 2003 was simply not acted on because of poor tracking and an office move, and holds that NASA 'has not yet met its burden of demonstrating that the search for documents was adequate.' Summary judgment was granted to NASA only on the withholding of two emails between FOIA officer Stephen McConnell and NASA attorney Bierbower under Exemption 5, which the court reviewed in camera on its own 22 February 2007 order. The court then ordered the parties to propose search and documentation procedures that would create a proper record. A Stipulation of Settlement in Part was signed by Judge Sullivan on 16 October 2007; NASA searched under supervision and filed joint status reports every sixty days from December 2007 to August 2009; the case was dismissed on 24 August 2009 on the parties' joint motion, the court finding NASA had met its settlement obligations. Along the way, NASA public liaison officer Steve McConnell testified that two boxes of papers from the period of the Kecksburg incident were missing.

entities.label: Cash v. United States, Civil Action No. H-84-348 (S.D. Tex.)
entities.sub: Federal Tort Claims Act suit over the 1980 Cash-Landrum encounter, 1984-1986
entities.desc: Betty Cash, Vickie Landrum and Colby Landrum sued the United States of America in the US District Court for the Southern District of Texas, Houston Division, over the 29 December 1980 encounter near Huffman, Texas. The original complaint and summonses were filed on 18 January 1984 under the Federal Tort Claims Act, 28 U.S.C. 1346(b) and 2671 et seq., the docket sheet classifying the cause as airplane product liability with damages of $5,000,000 - reported in the press as a $20 million action across the plaintiffs. Peter A. Gersten of Gagliardi, Torpes & Gersten of Tarrytown, New York was designated attorney in charge, with William C. Shead of Houston as local co-counsel; Assistant US Attorney Frank A. Conforti appeared for the government. The theory of the case was that the diamond-shaped object and the tandem-rotor helicopters escorting it were US government property or operations, and that the plaintiffs were injured by them. An amended complaint was filed, the government moved to dismiss and for summary judgment, and on 21 August 1986 Judge Ross N. Sterling entered an Order of Dismissal dismissing the action under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 12(b)(1), 12(b)(6) and 56. The government's position, and the ground on which the case ended, was that no such vehicle or operation was the United States'. Gersten later said the suit had been a bluff, brought in the hope of a quiet settlement of the medical bills. Two things about this docket matter to this board. First, it is the only time a UFO injury claim has reached a US federal court on the merits. Second, the Defense Department conducted an internal investigation into whether the object was a US military device, and no document from that investigation has ever surfaced.

entities.label: Kecksburg incident, 9 December 1965
entities.sub: Claimed object recovery, Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania
entities.desc: At about 4:44 p.m. EST on 9 December 1965 a brilliant fireball crossed Michigan, Ontario, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York, Indiana, Idaho and West Virginia; the FAA logged twenty-three pilot reports beginning at 4:44 p.m. and a seismograph twenty-five miles southwest of Detroit recorded the shock wave. Around 4:46 p.m., residents of Kecksburg, thirty miles southeast of Pittsburgh, reported blue smoke, vibration and a thump, and that something had come down in the woods. The Greensburg Tribune-Review reported that the area was 'immediately sealed off on the order of U.S. Army and State Police officials, in anticipation of a close inspection' and that state police had roped it off pending the arrival of Army engineers and possibly civilian scientists; a later edition ran 'Searchers Fail to Find Object'. Local witnesses collected over decades by Stan Gordon describe an acorn-shaped object about the size of a Volkswagen bearing hieroglyph-like markings, removed by flatbed truck. In December 2005 NASA stated that experts had examined metallic fragments from the area and determined they came from a Soviet satellite that had re-entered and broken up, but that the records of those findings had been lost in the 1980s. That statement is why the litigation happened. NASA's own current position undermines the satellite explanation: analysis of the fireball's photographs and sightings indicates a path too steep to be consistent with orbital re-entry, US Air Force tracking data indicate Cosmos 96's orbit decayed earlier than 21:43 UT on 9 December, and other analyses indicate definitively that it could not have been Cosmos 96. The structural fact this board records is that the cordon is documented in the contemporaneous local press, and the disposition of whatever was inside it is documented nowhere.

entities.label: Shag Harbour incident, 4 October 1967
entities.sub: Object impact and Canadian military underwater search, Nova Scotia
entities.desc: At about 11:20 p.m. Atlantic Daylight Time on 4 October 1967 at least eleven people saw a low-flying lit object descend into the water off Shag Harbour, Nova Scotia; witnesses reported a whistling sound, a whoosh and a loud bang. Laurie Wickens and four companions, driving on Highway 3, reported to the RCMP detachment at Barrington Passage that a large aircraft had gone into the water. Two RCMP officers reached the scene within about fifteen minutes and the Rescue Coordination Centre in Halifax was alerted; the object, still lit, sank before any rescue attempt. Local fishing boats and a Canadian Coast Guard cutter from Clark's Harbour searched and found no survivors, bodies or debris. By the next morning RCC Halifax had established that no commercial, private or military aircraft were missing anywhere along the eastern seaboard, in the Atlantic provinces or in New England, and sent a priority telex to the Royal Canadian Air Force 'Air Desk' in Ottawa - the office handling all civilian and military UFO reports - explicitly stating that conventional explanations had been dismissed and labelling it a UFO Report. The head of the Air Desk telexed Royal Canadian Navy headquarters recommending an underwater search, and the Navy tasked Fleet Diving Unit Atlantic, which combed the seafloor of the Gulf of Maine for three days beginning two days after the event. The final report says no trace was found. The Chronicle-Herald of 7 October 1967 ran Ray MacLeod's front-page story 'Could Be Something Concrete in Shag Harbour UFO - RCAF', quoting Squadron Leader Bain of the Air Desk saying the Air Force was 'very interested' and that 'the Shag Harbour incident is one of the few where we may get something concrete on it.' The 9 October follow-up, 'UFO Search Called Off', quoted the Navy: 'Not a trace... not a clue... not a bit of anything.' A summary of the event from Department of National Defence files is held at Library and Archives Canada. Shag Harbour is the strongest case in the whole retrieval literature on the criterion this board cares about most - the response is documented in government paper even though the object is not.

entities.label: Varginha incident, January 1996
entities.sub: Claimed humanoid capture and military transport, Minas Gerais, Brazil
entities.desc: At around 3:30 p.m. on 20 January 1996, three young women aged fourteen to twenty-two reported encountering an unknown being near a subdivision on Rua Dr. Benevenuto Braz Vieira in Varginha, Minas Gerais, Brazil - a large-headed biped with vein-like markings on the skin, three bumps on the head and red eyes, apparently injured or unsteady. Reports of UFO sightings in the preceding days, of military, police and fire service vehicle movements, of an unidentified animal in local woodland, of the death of a police officer and of unexplained deaths at the municipal zoo of a tapir, an ocelot and two grey brockets were subsequently woven by Brazilian ufologists into a claim that one or more living beings were captured by the Brazilian armed forces and taken to Campinas. Varginha is the most substantial non-US retrieval claim in the modern record and it has a feature the American cases mostly lack: an actual official inquiry that named names. In 2010 a Brazilian military inquiry concluded that the young women had encountered a mentally disabled man nicknamed 'Mudinho', Luiz Antonio de Paula; the commander of the 24th Military Police Battalion supplied photographs and stated the man's physical characteristics matched the description and that he had probably been crouching dirty by a wall in heavy rain. The inquiry further concluded that the presence of firefighters in Jardim Andere, the parking of Army trucks near a dealership for periodic maintenance, and the movement of Escola de Sargentos das Armas vehicles were real events incorrectly interpreted as a capture and transport operation. This board records the inquiry as the official position and notes what it is: an explanation of the vehicle movements offered fourteen years after the fact, which does not produce the underlying unit logs.

entities.label: Aztec, New Mexico claim, March 1948
entities.sub: Claimed 99-foot disc recovery, Hart Canyon; sourced to convicted fraudsters
entities.desc: The first crashed-saucer story to reach a mass audience, and the reason the whole genre carries a fraud provenance. Frank Scully's 1949 Variety columns and his 1950 Henry Holt book 'Behind the Flying Saucers' reported that in March 1948 a 99-foot disc containing sixteen small humanoid bodies made a controlled landing in Hart Canyon twelve miles northeast of Aztec, New Mexico, was taken by the military for secret research, ran on magnetic principles, came from Venus, carried concentrated food wafers and heavy water, and had every dimension divisible by nine. Scully's sources were Silas M. Newton and, behind the description 'more degrees than a thermometer', Leo A. Gebauer. Both were travelling the Four Corners selling oil-and-mineral 'doodlebug' detectors which they claimed were built on recovered alien technology; when San Francisco Chronicle reporter J. P. Cahn asked for a sample of the alien metal they produced ordinary aluminium; Cahn published in True in 1952 and again in 1956; and in 1953 both men were convicted of fraud after the millionaire Herman Flader pressed charges. From the mid-1950s to the early 1970s ufologists treated Aztec as dead. It was revived by Robert Spencer Carr in 1974, who claimed the bodies were held at 'Hangar 18' at Wright-Patterson - prompting Air Force denials that there is any Hangar 18 and observations that Carr's claims tracked the plot of the 1968 novel 'The Fortec Conspiracy' - and then by Leonard Stringfield in the late 1970s, who treated the craft as one of many held by the US military. Many of the details later attached to first-hand Roswell accounts, including material impervious to heat and bodies of 36 to 42 inches weighing around 40 pounds, entered the literature from Aztec.

The FBI has described it as a second- or third-hand claim it never investigated.

entities.label: Plains of San Agustin claim, July 1947
entities.sub: Claimed second 1947 crash site, 175 miles northwest of Roswell
entities.desc: The claim that a second craft came down in July 1947 on the Plains of San Agustin, a graben basin in Catron and Socorro Counties, New Mexico, about 175 miles northwest of Roswell, best known today as the site of the Very Large Array. It rests on three testimonies: two second-hand accounts from Vern Maltais and Alice Knight relaying what the soil conservation engineer Grady L. 'Barney' Barnett had told them before his death in 1969, and one first-hand account from Gerald Anderson, who came forward in 1990 claiming to have been a five-year-old rockhounding there. The claim entered the literature through Berlitz and Moore's 'The Roswell Incident' (1980), was central to Friedman and Berliner's 'Crash at Corona' (1992), and forced the Roswell literature into two-crash and three-crash constructions to reconcile a debris field near Corona with an intact craft 175 miles away. It was substantially dismantled from inside the field: Mark Rodeghier of CUFOS and Fred Whiting of the Fund for UFO Research published 'The Plains of San Agustin Controversy' in 1992 concluding against Anderson. The Air Force's 1997 report offers a specific alternative reading - that Maltais and Knight, three decades on, may have confused the Plains of San Agustin with San Agustin Pass or San Agustin Peak in the San Agustin Mountains, just outside White Sands Missile Range and the Jornada Test Range, where numerous anthropomorphic dummy balloon flights terminated and were recovered by uniformed teams who told civilians to leave.

entities.label: Kingman, Arizona claim, 1953
entities.sub: Claimed craft and single body recovery; source pseudonym 'Fritz Werner'
entities.desc: The 1953 Kingman, Arizona claim is the retrieval case with the cleanest documented chain of custody for its own testimony, and it is still only tier 2. It was first investigated and reported by the Massachusetts researcher Raymond E. Fowler, working from a source using the pseudonym 'Fritz Werner', an engineer who said he had been flown from an Air Force facility to a desert site under escort and shown a craft and a single small body, with each specialist restricted to his own area of examination and required to sign a secrecy agreement. Stringfield published the case as Abstract 6 in 'Retrievals of the Third Kind' (1978) and referenced it in 'Situation Red, The UFO Siege' (Doubleday, 1977) at pages 178-185. On 11 August 1980 Stringfield wrote to Fowler asking permission to put questions directly to Werner; the answers, dated 2 September 1980, are printed verbatim in Status Report III. Werner's replies are notable for what they concede: asked for facial detail on the deceased entity he answered that after twenty-seven years the details were 'pretty foggy' and that he might 'even be influenced by other descriptions I've seen or heard in the interim' - a witness volunteering, on the record, the exact contamination mechanism this board treats as the central problem of the retrieval corpus. The case is compartment-shaped in a way that fits the domain's premise - specialists shown only their own piece, sworn to secrecy, no one able to describe the whole - and it is unsupported by any document.

entities.label: Del Rio / Mexican border claim, 1948 or 1950
entities.sub: Claimed crashed craft and one body observed by an Air Force officer
entities.desc: One of the oldest claims in the retrieval corpus and one of the weakest, retained here because Stringfield indexed it and because it is a worked example of what an unresolvable case looks like. It appears in Stringfield's consolidated chronology as Item B-7 of Status Report II, entered as '1948 or 1950: Mexico, near Del Rio, Texas. Air Force officer observed crashed craft and one body' - a claim that cannot be dated to a year, cannot be placed on a side of an international border, and rests on a single unnamed source. The most-cited version in the wider literature is attributed to a retired officer, Robert B. Willingham, who over several decades gave accounts of a disc down near the Texas-Mexico border, with the date, the location and his own claimed rank and role varying materially between tellings and his stated service history contested against his record. This board does not carry the Willingham account as a claim because it cannot state a version of it that its own source has not contradicted. entities.label: Northern tier SAC base overflights, October-November 1975
entities.sub: Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom, Minot and Falconbridge; NORAD and NMCC records
entities.desc: The best-documented episode in the entire UFO-nuclear record, because the paper is the government's own and it was released. Over roughly a fortnight in late October and early November 1975, unidentified objects were reported over Strategic Air Command weapons storage and alert areas and over Minuteman missile fields at Loring AFB, Maine (27, 28 and 31 October), Wurtsmith AFB, Michigan (30 October), Malmstrom AFB, Montana (7-8 November), Minot AFB, North Dakota, and Canadian Forces Station Falconbridge, Ontario. A NORAD document dated 11 November 1975 records that reliable military personnel at all five installations had visually sighted suspicious objects. A Loring AFB teletype states that an unidentified object 'demonstrated a clear intent in the weapons storage area' - the phrase from which Fawcett and Greenwood took the title of their 1984 book. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's log for 7 November 1975 records the 341st SAC Command Post reporting sightings from missile sites M-1, L-3, LIMA and L-6 near Moore and Buffalo, Montana at 1035Z; the Harlow launch control facility observing an object illuminating the site driveway at 1203Z; site K-1 tracking a bright object through 10x50 binoculars at 1319Z; and L-1 at 1327Z reporting the object issuing a tubular black object, with surveillance unable to establish any track. The National Military Command Center's Memorandum for the Record of 8 November 1975, subject 'Unidentified Sightings', records that at 0253 EST Malmstrom received seven radar cuts on the height-finder radar between 9,500 and 15,500 feet with simultaneous ground witnesses reporting lights and jet engine noise, that cross-tell with the FAA revealed no jet aircraft within 100 nautical miles, that two F-106 interceptors from the 24th NORAD Region were scrambled at 0254 and airborne at 0257, and that at 0344 EST the objects could not be intercepted because the fighters had to stay above 12,000 feet over mountainous terrain. These documents reached the public because Citizens Against UFO Secrecy filed a FOIA request on 26 December 1977; the Office of the Assistant Secretary of Defense replied on 6 February 1978 identifying twenty-four documents held by the Office of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and after an internal argument over exempting raw unevaluated reporting, Assistant Secretary of Defense Thomas Ross determined no useful purpose would be served by withholding them.

Schmitt was its co-director of special investigations while co-writing the two Randle-Schmitt Roswell books; Kevin Randle has worked through it; Stringfield acknowledged its cooperation in Status Report VII; Allan Hendry investigated the Cash-Landrum case for it in 1981; and Stringfield records consulting its scientific director in November 1993 on the Roswell body count. Its most important single act on this board is negative: in 1992 CUFOS scientific director Mark Rodeghier joined Fred Whiting of the Fund for UFO Research to publish 'The Plains of San Agustin Controversy', an investigation that dismantled Gerald Anderson, the only first-hand witness to a claimed second 1947 crash site and a witness the field badly wanted to be true. An organisation that publishes findings against its own interest is producing evidence rather than advocacy, and this board weights it accordingly.

entities.label: Guy Hottel memorandum, 22 March 1950
entities.sub: FBI Washington Field Office memo on three recovered circular craft
entities.desc: A one-page memorandum written on 22 March 1950 by Guy Hottel, special agent in charge of the FBI's Washington Field Office, relaying a third-party account that an Air Force investigator had reported the recovery in New Mexico of three circular craft approximately fifty feet in diameter, each containing three humanoid bodies about three feet tall wearing metallic cloth, the recovery attributed to interference from a high-powered radar installation in the area. The memo ends: 'No further evaluation was attempted.' It became the most-viewed document on the FBI's Vault reading room when that was launched in April 2011, and the FBI has publicly characterised it as 'a second- or third-hand claim that we never investigated'. The document's status on this board is precise and should not be inflated: it is tier 1 as an artifact - a genuine FBI record of that date, publicly released, whose text says what it says - and tier 3 as evidence of a recovery, because its own author recorded that the Bureau did nothing with it. What it does establish is that by March 1950 an account of multiple recovered discs with small occupants was circulating at a level that reached an FBI field office SAC in writing, two months before Scully's book appeared, and that the Bureau's response was to file it.

entities.label: Kecksburg, Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania

entities.desc: An unincorporated village in Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, about thirty miles southeast of Pittsburgh, and the claimed site of the 9 December 1965 recovery. The contemporaneous Greensburg Tribune-Review reported that the wooded area where something was said to have come down was immediately sealed off on the order of US Army and State Police officials in anticipation of a close inspection, with Army engineers and possibly civilian scientists expected; a subsequent edition reported that searchers failed to find any object. Kecksburg is the geographic anchor of the only successful FOIA litigation in this domain: the records Leslie Kean sued NASA for in 2003 were records about this location and this date, and the court found in 2007 that NASA had not adequately searched for them.
